PULLMAN – Here is a first look at Washington State’s road game against Oregon State on Saturday afternoon.

What isit? Still looking for its first FBS win of the season, WSU (1-5, 0-2 Pac-12) heads to Corvallis to take on Oregon State (4-2, 2-0) in a matchup of the two legacy Pac-12 schools. The teams find themselves on opposite ends of the conference standings – the Cougars at the bottom, the Beavers at the top – using one of the country’s most potent offenses to enter this matchup on a four-game winning streak.

It’s a homecoming of sorts for Cougar defensive coordinator Trent Bray, who spent a large chunk of his coaching career with the Beavers, including as their head coach for the 2024 season and part of the 2025 campaign before being fired.

It will also be the first start for WSU QB Owen Eshelman, who is taking over the starting duties and replacing Caden Pinnick, Cougar coach Kirby Moore announced on Monday.

Where is it? Reser Stadium in Corvallis.

When is it? Kickoff is set for 3 p.m.

Where can I watch it? USA Network will broadcast the game.

Who is favored? WSU opened as a 171/2-point underdog.

How did the Cougars fare last week? A lot had to happen for WSU to lose its road game against Utah State last weekend, but the Cougars pulled it off, blowing a two-score halftime lead in a 17-16 defeat. The Cougs lost two fumbles, one from quarterback Caden Pinnick and one from tight end Jack Pedersen, both of which turned into Aggie touchdowns in the second half.

WSU, which scored only its fourth touchdown in five FBS games in this game, could not generate any consistent offense in the second half. After getting two field goals from kicker Jack Stevens and a long touchdown rush from Leo Pulalasi in the first half, that production vanished in the second, and the Cougars totaled just 64 total yards of offense in the final two quarters.

All told, it was more of the same from WSU and Pinnick, who is now one of only three quarterbacks in the country to attempt at least 150 passes and total less than 1,000 yards. That highlights one of the biggest flaws in his game, which has hampered his offense: He can’t or won’t stretch the field vertically, forcing the Cougars to try and grind out long drives, which has not been a recipe for success in the long run.

Pinnick was sacked three times in that game, which makes 21 times on the season, one of the highest marks in the country. Only two other teams have given up more. Complicating things on that front for WSU was an ankle injury to left tackle Ashton Tripp, who exited the game in the first quarter. He was replaced by Washington transfer Maximus McCree, who was dinged for two false start penalties.

On the other side of the ball, WSU’s defense turned in another strong showing, getting one sack apiece from defensive tackle Jirah Leaupepetele and defensive end Linus Zunk, whose team held the Aggies to just two field goals in the first half. WSU held USU quarterback Grady Brosterhous to just 150 yards passing, including just one touchdown pass, but that score helped the hosts draw within one score. Late in the fourth quarter, after Pedersen coughed up a fumble, the Cougars were dealt a short field and couldn’t keep the Aggies from taking the lead on a short touchdown rush.

In head coach Kirby Moore’s first game calling plays, WSU did generate some offense in the first half, including grinding out a 15-play, 84-yard series. On those drives, Pinnick stayed within himself and trusted his playmakers. But the Cougars couldn’t translate that to the second half.

Scouting Oregon State … In head coach JaMarcus Shephard’s first season, the Beavers have been one of the top surprises in all of college football, bursting onto the scene with one of the best offenses nationwide. Quarterback Braden Atkinson leads the country in both passing yards per game (376) and passing touchdowns (21), finding a reliable target in true freshman Jesse Legree, who is emerging as one of the best receivers in the country.

Legree, the Pac-12 Freshman of the Week all six weeks of the season, will pose serious problems for the Cougar secondary. Listed at 5-foot-10 and 170 pounds, Legree has hauled in 38 catches for 932 yards and 12 touchdowns, leading the country in the latter two categories.

Fresh off a 66-14 dismantling of San Diego State, OSU can seemingly do no wrong. Running back AJ Newberry, a transfer from Vanderbilt, has tallied 326 rushing yards and three scores, while fellow tailback Cornell Hatcher Jr. has added 149 yards and three of his own touchdowns. Make no mistake: This is one of the country’s best offenses.

“He’s a really good player,” Moore said of Legree. “You see him with the ball in space, obviously taking the top off a number of times as well. I think it’s about playing team defense. Obviously, communication is gonna be really important: Where he’s at, whether he’s in the slot, whether he’s outside, left, right. The pass rush has to help out the coverage. The coverage has gotta help out the pass rush. I think Coach Bray is doing a good job right now with our guys, making sure they’re all on the same page.”

The Beavers have also done well to involve their tight ends: Utah Tech transfer Eric Olsen has racked up 27 catches for 280 yards and three touchdowns, while Central Michigan transfer DeCorion Temple has 20 receptions for 169 yards and two scores. Sprinkle in some production from receivers Aeyron Hampton and Aaron Butler, the latter a transfer from Texas, and you get the Beavers’ high-powered offense.

What happened last time? In a rare scheduling quirk, WSU and Oregon State played twice last season, once in Corvallis and once in Pullman. The Beavers won their home matchup, 10-7, while the Cougars returned the favor in Pullman, winning that one 32-8.

This will be WSU’s third time in the last three years playing in Corvallis.

Washington State.title: Boise State, OSU on top, with WSU taking over the cellar | Pac-12 power rankings
Washington State.summary:
The Pac-12 football power rankings are published each Sunday on the Hotline and consider both the latest results and season-long performance. Call it an objectively subjective look at the state of the conference. If you’re unhappy with the order, email us at the address below … or play better. For comparative purposes, we have included the placement of each team in last week’s rankings.

Based on postseason impact, the most significant Week 6 result in the Pac-12 was Boise State’s victory over Fresno State.

After that: Oregon State’s wipeout of San Diego State.

Next on the list? It came outside the conference: UNLV’s escape against North Dakota State, which handed the Bison their first loss and reduced the likelihood of the Mountain West producing an undefeated champion.

The 2026 season has reached the midway point, which means the time for scoreboard watching is upon us.

For the Pac-12, the calculation is fairly simple:

Any zero- or one-loss teams from the Mountain West, Mid-American, American, Conference USA or Sun Belt are potential obstacles in pursuit of the berth in the College Football Playoff that has been reserved for the top team in the Group of Six.

There are no guarantees. Two losses could become the threshold by the end of Championship Weekend in early December.

But for now, our focus is the array of teams that could finish 13-0 or 12-1.

There are nine.

American: Memphis, UTSA and Florida Atlantic.

Conference USA: Liberty

Mid-American: none

Mountain West: Air Force, New Mexico and North Dakota State

Sun Belt: James Madison and Georgia State

Because of upcoming head-to-head matchups, that list will shrink. For example, New Mexico plays both NDSU and Air Force. Also, UTSA plays Florida Atlantic.

But by our calculations, it’s reasonable to expect a few teams outside the Pac-12 to end the season 13-0 or 12-1. Some combination of Memphis, Liberty, James Madison and New Mexico is the most likely.

Of course, the Pac-12 only has one team capable of clearing that bar: Boise State (5-1). A second defeat would cast the Broncos down to the realm of two-loss teams and narrow their path into the CFP.

Then again, it’s worth accounting for the unexpected. Depending on results across the Group of Six, it’s possible that a second loss for Boise State could become the optimal outcome for the Pac-12.

We’ll explore that scenario later this month.

To the power rankings …

(All times Pacific)

1. Boise State (5-1/2-0)

Result: won at Fresno State 38-31

Next up: idle

Comment: The drive that produced the key field goal in the final minutes – and a two-score lead – covered 13 plays. All of them were runs. It was the most Boise State of all Boise State drives. And there was nothing Fresno State could do to stop it. (Last week: 1)

2. Oregon State (4-2/2-0)

Result: beat San Diego State 66-14

Next up: vs. Washington State (3 p.m. on USA Network)

Comment: What if the Beavers played Boise State on a neutral field in eastern Oregon this week? (Burns seems like a nice location.) Our hunch is the oddsmakers would make the Broncos a slight favorite: 2.5 points or thereabouts. And that’s roughly one-fifth of what we would have expected prior to the season. (Last week: 2)

3. Fresno State (4-2/1-1)

Result: lost to Boise State 38-31

Next up: at San Diego State (7:30 p.m. on CBS Sports Network)

Comment: All hope is not lost, but the Bulldogs must handle Oregon State on Halloween or risk getting boxed out of the conference championship game. And they probably can’t afford to lose elsewhere. (Last week: 3)

4. Colorado State (2-3/0-1)

Result: did not play

Next up: at Texas State (Thursday at 5 p.m. on CBS Sports Network)

Comment: With Jim Mora and the Rams idle ahead of the rare Thursday game – college football has largely abandoned the day because of the NFL – the Pac-12 was not nearly as interesting a place. (Last week: 4)

5. San Diego State (2-4/1-1)

Result: lost at Oregon State 66-14

Next up: vs. Fresno State (7:30 p.m. on CBS Sports Network)

Comment: Was losing defensive coordinator Rob Aurich (to Nebraska) the most significant staff defection any of the eight programs suffered last winter? You could make that case with 66 pieces of evidence. (Last week: 5)

6. Texas State (2-3/0-1)

Result: did not play

Next up: vs. Colorado State (Thursday at 5 p.m. on CBS Sports Network)

Comment: If the Bobcats lose this week, the bowl math will require them to win in either Boise or Corvallis or on the Flex Saturday at the end of the season. And they are scheduled for a road game. (Last week: 6)

7. Utah State (2-4/1-1)

Result: beat Washington State 17-16

Next up: idle

Comment: Bronco Mendenhall, drawing water from stone once again. With a few more wins, he might warrant consideration for Pac-12 Coach of the Year/non-JaMarcus Shephard division. (Last week: 8)

8. Washington State (1-5/0-2)

Result: lost at Utah State 17-16

Next up: at Oregon State (3 p.m. on USA Network)

Comment: We mentioned on social media that the Cougars seem destined for a 2-10 season and readers wondered where the second win would come. There’s enough mediocrity in the conference for WSU to stumble into another victory. Maybe. (Last week: 7)

Washington State.title: 3 lingering thoughts from WSU's road loss to Utah State | Rewind
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – In his first 10 months on the job, Washington State coach Kirby Moore has made at least one thing crystal clear.

In public settings, he doesn’t want to single out his quarterback.

As the Cougars’ slow start to the season continues, reaching 1-5 after a surprising road loss to Utah State Friday night, Moore has demonstrated that he doesn’t want to talk about quarterback Caden Pinnick in specifics. When given the opportunity, he turns his answer into a referendum on his entire offense, addressing systemic issues rather than individuals.

Here’s a sample: In his postgame news conference on Friday, he was asked about his concern level with Pinnick, who has now lost seven turnovers and doesn’t look comfortable letting it fly in the pocket.

“Well, my concern level with the offense is we’re not scoring enough points,” said Moore, who called plays for the first time in Friday’s game, taking over those duties from offensive coordinator Matt Miller. “Yes, there’s a quarterback piece of that. There’s an offensive line piece of that. There’s a skill piece of that. There’s running backs. Making sure we’re seeing it how we saw it in practice. So all of that, we gotta work like heck to score more points.”

Moore was not wrong at all. The Cougars committed 13 penalties for 113 yards. Outside of running back Leo Pulalasi’s 54-yard touchdown sprint in the second quarter, they generated only 23 rushing yards on 18 carries from their running back trio. And thanks to left tackle Ashton Tripp’s ankle injury in the first quarter, things got even shakier up front in WSU’s pre-snap operations.

But as WSU prepares for its next game, a road test against surging Oregon State next weekend, the questions are only going to grow louder around Pinnick.

Here are three thoughts from WSU’s loss to Utah State.

1. Coaches may not have any choice but to move away from Pinnick

At this point, Moore and Miller may not have much choice but to pivot away from Pinnick and start a new quarterback against Oregon State, whether it’s redshirt freshman Owen Eshelman or redshirt sophomore Julian Dugger.

In Friday’s game, Pinnick completed 23 of 36 passes … for just 156 yards. He did not complete a single pass further than 9 yards downfield, according to Pro Football Focus, highlighting one of his main weaknesses: He either can’t or won’t stretch the field vertically. The only times he looked further downfield included when Utah State had jumped offsides, offering a free play, and one key miss (more on that in a moment).

That paves the way for the stat that paints this picture best: Pinnick is now one of just two quarterbacks in the country to attempt at least 150 passes and total less than 1,000 yards. The other is Middle Tennessee’s Roman Gagliano. In other words, Pinnick is having little trouble completing passes, but never further than about 9 yards, which has hampered the Cougars’ offense in huge ways.

Pinnick did look sharper in the first half, though. He played his game, completing short routes and letting his playmakers do their thing, including a nice juke and run from tight end Trey Leckner in his second game back from injury. He made shrewd reads, including when to bail from the pocket and run upfield, doing so for a couple first downs.

But in the second half, Pinnick was simply missing throws. His biggest miss came in the third frame, when he dropped back and spotted a wide open Pulalasi, who had nothing but green grass ahead of him. But Pinnick couldn’t deliver an accurate throw and it fell incomplete.

How can the Cougars solve that problem? Pinnick has provided a six-game sample of his abilities, so there may not be a way other than making a change at quarterback. On Friday, they did give one snap to Dugger, who carved out a 5-yard gain, underscoring his strengths on the ground. But to unlock a more compelling passing attack, they might consider Eshelman, whose arm talent could do just that.

“There (were) plays for Julian,” Moore said. “Obviously, Owen had more reps in practice this week. The first half, I thought Caden did a nice job of moving the ball. We just didn’t finish there in the red zone.”

Would either of those quarterbacks perform meaningfully better? It’s impossible to know, but it’s becoming clear that the Cougars’ offense might not be able to improve as currently constructed.

2. The Cougars have to be better in their pre-snap operation

To Moore’s point, WSU’s offensive issues were hardly limited to just the quarterback. Ten of the Cougars’ 13 penalties came on offense, including five holding penalties, several of which wiped out key plays.

But WSU’s pre-snap penalties were killer, too. The Cougs were whistled for three false starts and one delay of game penalty, which came in the second quarter, right after the Aggies were called for unsportsmanlike conduct. Pinnick and the WSU offense were coming off a dead ball, a penalty situation. And the Cougs couldn’t get their play off in time.

For WSU, it didn’t help that in the first quarter, left tackle Ashton Tripp went down with what Moore called a “pretty good ankle sprain.” He was out for the rest of the game, so in came Washington transfer Maximus McCree, whose lack of playing time seemed curious earlier in the season. He acquitted himself well as a blocker, but he was also dinged for two false start penalties, the first of which led to a field goal from Jack Stevens and the second of which later resulted in a punt.

Earlier in the game, after Pinnick took a late-hit penalty as he slid to the ground, the Cougars had more pre-snap chaos. With about five seconds on the play clock, Pinnick tried to change the play, leading three receivers to move around. That happened far too late in the play clock, forcing WSU to burn a timeout.

3. Jack Stevens is fully back

It’s officially safe to say: Jack Stevens is still the same guy who delivered an incredible 2025 campaign. He has now connected on six straight field goals, including three in Friday’s game, his longest a 50-yarder – the second straight game he’s connected from 50 yards, tying his career-long.

Stevens, who has put his 1-for-5 start in the past to deliver a 7-for-12 mark on the year, is back as a real weapon for this WSU offense. Things weren’t always his fault earlier in the year – he had two field goals blocked, one of which was a product of a missed block on the offensive line – but he did look shaky.

Now he looks consistent and confident, two of the best traits a kicker can possess. In a WSU offense that is still scuffling, averaging just 12.6 points per game, Stevens could play a key role if the Cougars can find a way to turn things around.

Washington State.title: Washington State offense continues to spiral in agonizing loss at Utah State | Instant reactions
Washington State.summary:
Coming off one of its worst losses in recent memory, Washington State stumbled to another humiliating defeat, blowing what appeared to be a comfortable lead and falling 17-16 to fellow Pac-12 bottomfeeder Utah State on Friday night at Maverik Stadium in Logan, Utah.

The Cougars’ offense was unwatchable for the large part of the game, even with coach Kirby Moore taking over playcalling duties from offensive coordinator Matt Miller, who failed to get the unit moving in last weekend’s dismal display against Fresno State. As has been the case for much of what has become a lost season, the Cougars’ defense had a respectable performance squandered and WSU slipped to 1-5 overall and 0-2 in the rebuilt Pac-12 Conference.

Wheels are off

After WSU fell flat last weekend against Fresno State, many fans were rightfully in full-blown panic mode, and Friday’s effort only made matters worse.

The Cougars are off to a disastrous start under their new staff in the new Pac-12. They were expected to be contenders in this refashioned conference with a seemingly soft schedule. WSU saw an opportunity to establish itself as one of the conference’s top dogs. Instead, the Cougs are one of its worst teams. And they face Pac-12 contenders Oregon State and Boise State in the next two weeks. Any bowl hopes are almost certainly out the window.

To restore some amount of faith in the fanbase, the Cougars absolutely could not afford to lose to lowly Utah State (2-4, 1-1). The Aggies, like WSU, have one of the worst offenses in the country. The Aggies lost to FCS Idaho State to open their season. The Aggies were just steamrolled last weekend by Boise State, a team that was supposed to be a good rivalry match for WSU.

WSU needed to win to preserve some hope in this season. But the wheels are fully off now.

Something else needs to change offensively

WSU’s offense was not quite as bad as last week. But it was close. Quarterback Caden Pinnick, the receivers, the run game – nothing was inspiring.

The Cougars had few openings in the ground game, save for Leo Pulalasi’s 54-yard scoring scamper in the second quarter – a play that only happened because a Utah State defender committed an unsportsmanlike penalty after the Aggies sacked Pinnick on third down on the previous play.

Take away that run, and WSU managed 47 yards on 31 carries, good for a whopping 1.5 yards per attempt.

Following the season’s trend, Pinnick couldn’t complete passes downfield. He settled almost entirely for checkdowns or designed receiver screens. He threw 36 passes and finished with just 156 yards and committed a costly turnover – already his seventh of the year. At some point, the Cougars need to consider their other options.

Whatever changes Moore brought as the new playcaller clearly didn’t bring results, as the Cougars’ offense continued to trend downward, putting up the kinds of numbers WSU hasn’t seen since the Paul Wulff era. And it obviously didn’t help that the offense committed 10 penalties, a few of them costly errors in scoring position.

To be fair, it seemed like the Cougars offense operated with some semblance of rhythm for parts of the first half. They scored (field goals) on their first three drives, logged their first touchdown in two weeks and totaled 193 yards – more than they mustered in all of last week’s loss.

Then the Cougs fell apart in the second half, recording only 64 yards, no points, averaging less than 1 yard per carry, 2.2 yards per play and going 1 of 8 on third downs. They led by 13 entering the second half, but couldn’t put any offense together to finish the deal and had no answers when Utah State went ahead in the fourth quarter. The Cougs’ offense practically handed it to Utah State, committing two turnovers (fumbles by Pinnick and tight end Jack Pedersen) in their own territory to gift Utah State a momentum-turning touchdown, and later, the go-ahead score.

Aggies weren’t good, either

It’s not like Utah State found some groove and turned into a competent team. The Aggies also looked miserable throughout this one. Their offense only moved in the second half when they were given two possessions on short fields. Utah State totaled 236 yards, 21 fewer than WSU, which had possession for about 11 more minutes than the hosts.

The Aggies’ quarterback, Grady Brosterhous, completed just 11 of 26 passes for 150 yards. Those are not winning numbers. Many of his throws were just plain off-target. But he got enough chances that eventually, some of them hit.

Utah State averaged 2.9 yards per carry. Again, not a good number. The Cougars’ interior defense mostly held, but could only preserve a low score for so long. Will the offense ever reward its defensive counterparts?

Washington State.title: Utah State linebacker Asher Cunningham makes game-changing plays | Difference makers
Washington State.summary:
Asher Cunningham

The junior middle linebacker made the most important plays for Utah State, forcing two turnovers – the second one led to the Aggies’ go-ahead touchdown midway through the fourth quarter. Cunningham stripped Cougars tight end Jack Pedersen just before his knee hit the turf on a third-down play with under eight minutes left, then the linebacker pounced on the ball deep in WSU territory, setting Utah State up to take its first lead. Cunningham also laid a hard hit on WSU quarterback Caden Pinnick in the third quarter, knocking the ball free. It was recovered by the Aggies, and they scored a touchdown five plays later to flip the game’s momentum. An Elon transfer, Cunningham finished with a game-high and career-high 17 tackles, half a sack and two tackles for loss in the run game. The 6-2, 240-pounder now has 52 tackles for the season, which will likely land him in the top 20 nationally after the weekend’s slate of games.

Jirah Leaupepetele

A nose tackle’s efforts often go unappreciated. But the 349-pound Leaupepetele deserves some recognition after his gap-plugging effort for a Cougars defense that didn’t surrender much on inside running plays. Leaupepetele overpowered blockers for two solo stops at the line of scrimmage. The junior Eastern Washington transfer also recorded his first full sack of the season during the third quarter, pushing through the Utah State line to wrap up Grady Brosterhous on a second-and-13, effectively stopping a key possession for the Aggies, who trailed by six points and appeared to have momentum. With under three minutes remaining in the game, on a critical third-and-short, Leaupepetele stood up his blocker and brought down Aggies running back Javen Jacobs just before the line to gain, forcing a punt and keeping WSU alive. Leaupepetele tied for third on the team with five total tackles.

Washington State.title: Washington State collapses in shocking loss to Utah State | Recap and highlights
Washington State.summary:
LOGAN, Utah — Kirby Moore kept his usual poker face on the sideline, trying to tune everything out, focusing on his playsheet. Things were falling apart around him at Maverik Stadium, where Utah State had just taken the lead on his Washington State team, so the hosts’ band played and the fans bellowed and the navy-clad Aggies celebrated this late-game swing.

Here on Friday night, WSU had been in control for so long, but Utah State had just wrested it back. In his first time with full playcalling duties, Moore studied his call sheet, trying to find the right combination of plays to help his Cougars bounce back.

Either Moore couldn’t do so, or the Cougs couldn’t execute the calls, or it was some brutal mixture of the two that led to WSU’s 17-16 loss to Utah State. Either way, it’s the third straight setback for WSU, which will have some major questions to answer after a second straight anemic outing on offense in a season replete with them.

For the game, the Cougars lost two turnovers, both of which led to Aggie touchdowns. Quarterback Caden Pinnick was responsible for one, a fumble, while tight end Jack Pedersen lost his own fumble in the fourth quarter. It’s the worst loss of the season for WSU, which committed 13 penalties for 133 yards in this loss, a key reason why the Cougars failed to score in the second half and couldn’t take down a Utah State team that entered with just one win.

Late in the fourth frame, the Cougs had two chances to drive down the field and take the lead, and they failed to do so both times. They had to punt the ball away on both occasions, even on their second drive, when the Aggies elected to punt the ball away on fourth-and-inches near midfield.

Utah State, which scored one touchdown on a pass in the third frame and another on a short rush in the fourth, held WSU to only 64 total yards in the second half. For the game, Pinnick completed 23 of 36 passes for just 156 yards, underscoring the way his lack of a convincing deep ball has hampered his offense.

Headed into this game, it was uncertain whether Pinnick would start this game, following his two-turnover outing the previous weekend against Fresno State. After that game, Moore said everything would be up for reevaluation with his offense, but he wound up rolling out all the same starters, including the quarterback.

In Friday’s game, WSU (1-5, 0-2 Pac-12) did give one play to fellow quarterback Julian Dugger, who carved out a five-yard gain. He then came out of the game, never to return.

Complicating things for WSU was an injury to left tackle Ashton Tripp, who came out of the game in the first quarter and returned with his left foot in a boot, wearing warmup gear. Washington transfer Maximus McCree took his place for the rest of the game.

WSU broke its drought of five straight quarters without a touchdown in the second frame, when running back Leo Pulalasi took a shotgun handoff and darted to his left, taking advantage of key blocks from offensive lineman Jonny Lester and Noah Dunham to burst into the open field, jetting all the way to the end zone, a 54-yard saunter.

On the sideline, Pulalsi took off his helmet and unleashed a primal scream, celebrating his first touchdown in nearly two calendar years. In his four years in Pullman, Pulalasi has found himself near the end of the Cougars’ running back rotation.

Utah State drew back within one score in the third quarter, when Brosterhous stepped up in the pocket and laced one to the corner of the end zone for receiver Eli Wood, who leapt to make an acrobatic catch. He fell out of bounds immediately. Replay showed that Wood bobbled the ball on his way out of bounds, and if the play were reviewed by officials, it’s possible they would have seen enough to overturn it.

But officials did not review it, and the touchdown stood. With that score, the Aggies trimmed the Cougars’ lead to 16-10.

Then in the fourth quarter, after Pedersen fumbled deep in his team’s own territory, Utah State took over with great field position. Three plays later, USU running back Javen Jacobs plunged into the end zone, handing the hosts a 17-16 lead.

WSU returns to action next Saturday, traveling to face Oregon State in Corvallis, where the Cougars have not won since 2018.

BOX SCORE

Key moments

Utah State runs clock out, comes back to beat WSU

4th, 0:00 – USU 17, WSU 16: A disappointing first season for coach Kirby Moore has somehow gotten worse. Utah State picks up a first down and runs the clock out to beat WSU in Logan, Utah.

The Cougars were shutout in the second half. Both touchdowns it gave up were on short fields after turnovers.

WSU drops to 1-5, and 0-2 in the Pac-12. It may be some time before things get better with Oregon State and Boise State next on WSU’s schedule.

So much for that

4th, 1:43 – USU 17, WSU 16: Caden Pinnick is sacked on first down and on third down completes a pass, but its called back for holding. WSU punts to the USU 29 with all three timeouts. Defense needs another stop.

One more try for WSU

4th, 2:40 – USU 17, WSU 16: The defense did its job. Caden Pinnick and the Cougars trot onto the field at their own 25 after a three-and-out. WSU has all three timeouts.

Cougars forced to punt

4th, 5:13 – USU 17, WSU 16: Caden Pinnick’s short pass on third-and-5 is swatted down at the line of scrimmage. Max Dean punts 40 yards to the USU 38, where the Cougars defense needs to come up with a quick stop.

Aggies take the lead

4th, 6:22 – USU 17, WSU 16: Utah State takes its first lead of the night on a 2-yard run from Javen Jacobs. The Aggies quickly took advantage of the turnover setting up the score on a 17-yard pass from Grady Brosterhous to Javon Robinson.

Both of Utah State’s touchdowns have come quickly after a WSU turnover. Cougars will now have to press for a response.

Another costly fumble

4th, 7:55 – WSU 16, USU 10: For the second time tonight the Cougars have fumbled on their own side of the field. Tight end Jack Pedersen gave up the ball on third down in a group of USU defenders. The Aggies recovered at the WSU 19. The original ruling of down by contact was overturned by replay review.

WSU had a big 19-yard run from Leo Pulalasi wiped out by holding on first down setting the drive back.

The Aggies have a great chance to take the lead.

Penalty bails out WSU

4th, 10:09 – WSU 16, USU 10: Aggies were driving deep into WSU territory when coach Broncos Mendenhall was called for an unsportsmanlike conduct penalty that set up a third-and-20 and ultimately pushed his team out of field goal range.

Cougars gets the ball back at their own 12 after a punt.

Mendenhall was asking for a pass interference against WSU and appeared to say, “come on” to the sideline official who then threw the flag.

Utah State receiver Demick Starling had a big catch for 41 yards to start the threatening drive.

Another chance for the Aggies

4th, 13:19 – WSU 16, USU 10: Cougars get the ball back as the defense continues to stand strong, but WSU’s next drive stalls just out of field goal range and Max Dean’s punt goes into the end zone for a touchback.

Cougars have largely dominated this game, but Utah State has a chance to drive and take the lead for the first time.

More self-inflicted wounds

3rd, 3:17 – WSU 16, USU 10: Penalties continue to hurt the Cougars offense as an illegal formation wipes out a 37-yard run from Maxwell Wood. On the next play Caden Pinnick missed a wide open Leo Pulalasi on a play that would have gone for a big gain.

WSU is forced to punt after Pinnick is sacked for a loss of 9 on third down. Utah State takes back over at its 22. 

Aggies right back in it

3rd, 7:08 – WSU 16, USU 10: Utah State takes advantage of the turnover as Eli Wood makes a sensational catch in the side of the end zone on a 27-yard pass from Grady Brosterhous. Wood adjusted his body and just got a toe in as he bobbled the pass. 

Brosterhous has largely struggled completing 7 of 20 attempts for 84 yards, but gave his receiver the chance to make a huge play.

Big drive coming up for the Cougars offense.

Bad time for a turnover

3rd, 8:59 – WSU 16, USU 3: Caden Pinnick fakes a reverse on a designed keeper and the ball pops free in a mass of Utah State defenders. Aggies take over in WSU territory.

Unfortunate timing for the Cougars, who were trying to convert on third and short. WSU’s defense will need to stand strong and not let the Aggies build any momentum.

Nothing going to open second half

3rd, 13:26 – WSU 16, USU 3: Cougars go three-and-out to open the second half. Pinnick took a shot on a wheel route when he had tight end Trey Leckner open on a drag route. Then Leo Pulalasi was strung out on a run to the left side for no gain when he could have cut up field for positive yardage. And then Aggies blew up a wide receiver screen for a loss of 4.

Utah State takes over near midfield after a short punt.

Cougars up at halftime

Washington State holds a 16-3 lead over Utah State thanks to some solid defense and a big play from Leo Pulalasi.

The Cougars running back broke off a 54-yard touchdown run late in the second quarter. Jack Stevens also has three field goals for WSU.

WSU has held Utah State quarterback Grady Brosterhous to 4-for-16 passing for 51 yards. Utah State is 2 of 8 on third downs and were stopped on a fourth down conversion attempt.

WSU will receive to start the second half.

Two more punts

2nd, 1:36 – WSU 16, USU 3: Cougars unable to extend their lead after getting the ball back. Aggies have one more shot from their own 25 before halftime.

Pulalasi breaks it open

2nd, 3:32 – WSU 16, USU 3: The Cougars hardly had any traction with their running backs, but Leo Pulalasi just changed that in one play, running through a big hole on a zone run to the left side for a 54-yard touchdown.

The Cougars were stopped on the drive when Caden Pinnick was sacked on third down, but David Kabongo was called for unsportsmanlike conduct and Pulalasi made him pay on the next play.

Pinnick had been asked to do almost everything himself leading up to the big run. Cougars now in control and will get the ball after halftime.  

Cougars get fourth down stop

2nd, 5:49 – WSU 9, USU 3: After two straight three-and-outs, WSU gets the ball back at midfield. Utah State goes for it on fourth-and-3 and QB Grady Brosterhous is flushed from the pocket and tries to run for the first, but steps out of bounds just shy of the line to gain.

Stevens good from deep

2nd, 11:10 – WSU 9, USU 3: Kicker Jack Stevens has officially put his early-season struggles behind him as he boots a 50-yard field goal for his third of the night.

Cougars set back by multiple procedural penalties on that drive, now up to 6 penalties for 50 yards in the game. Caden Pinnick did well to extend the drive with a third-down scramble that ended in a personal foul to set WSU up in opposing territory.

Field goal battle continues

2nd, 14:38 – WSU 6, USU 3: Kian Afrookhteh’s second attempt is good, this time from 48 yards. Aggies picked up a big gain through the air at the end of the third quarter, but Grady Grosterhous fires three straight incompletions to end the drive.

The Utah State QB is 2-for-8 for 39 yards. 

 Stevens converts again

1st, 1:02 – WSU 6, USU 0: Cougars offense looks crips on a 54-yard drive that stalls on a holding penalty. Jack Stevens hits a 43-yard field goal to extend WSU’s lead.

The Cougars were effective in the quick passing game, converting on two third downs. Quarterback Caden Pinnick looks more comfortable with a few completions under his belt. He has completed 6 of 8 attempts for 53 yards and picks up a couple of nice gains with his legs eluding pressure in the pocket.

WSU’s conventional running game isn’t gaining much traction. Pinnnick leads with three carries for 17 yards and backup QB Julian Dugger came in to run for a gain of six. WSU’s three running backs have four attempts for minus-1 yard.

Utah State misses field goal

1st, 10:22 – WSU 3, USU 0: Aggies come up empty after a solid drive as Kian Afrookhteh pulls a 39-yard attempt from the left hash.

Utah State picked up 32 yards and a pass interference penalty. Rushing back Javen Jacobs handled three carries for 23 yards, but his draw on third-and-7 from the WSU 21 was wrapped up by Keith Brown for no gain.

Cougars settle for field goal, take lead

1st, 13:26 – WSU 3, USU 0: Cougars manage just three yards after the fumble recovery: A Tank Hawkins rush for 2 yards, incomplete pass to an open Braden Ganashamoorthy and 1-yard run by Maxwell Woods.

Jack Stevens converts the 40-yard attempt to get on the board, but WSU should have done more with that opportunity.

Utah State fumbles opening kick

Perfect start for the Cougars, who after winning the toss and deferring to the second half, pounce on a fumble by return man Noah White at the USU 25. Cougars have great field position for head coach Kirby Moore’s first drive as playcaller.

Pinnick repping with starters

Washington State seems content with keeping Caden Pinnick as its starting quarterback. Coach Kirby Moore indicated earlier this week that everything would be up for reevaluation when asked about a change at QB.

Pinnick has been taking first-team reps during warmups ahead of tonight’s game at Utah State. Pinnick has started every game this season for the Cougars, completing 87 of 142 attempts for 796 yards, three touchdowns and five interceptions.

Pregame

Washington State is hoping its first season in the new-look Pac-12 doesn’t turn into one to forget.

The Cougars (1-4, 0-1 Pac-12) have had plenty to work on during a short week following Saturday’s dreary 26-6 loss to Fresno State in Pullman.

After the worst offensive output of the season, first-year head coach Kirby Moore is taking over playcalling duties for tonight’s game at Utah State (1-4, 0-1), kicking off at 6 p.m. on The CW (KSKN). 

The Cougars and Aggies have had similarly disappointing starts to the season. Utah State earned its lone win against Troy on Sept. 26, lost to FCS Idaho State to open the season and dropped its Pac-12 opener to Boise State 37-18 last week.

Utah State is favored by 5½ points. A loss for either team would shade their outlook for the rest of the season.

Tale of the tape

Series history

Washington State holds a 4-2 all-time record over Utah State, taking the last two meetings in Pullman in 2024 and in the Famous Idaho Potato Bowl in 2025. The Aggies rallied to beat the Cougars in 2021, opening a lackluster September that, along with a refusal to comply with state COVID-19 mandates, would lead to coach Nick Rolovich’s firing.

Washington State.title: Why Utah State will beat Washington State
Washington State.summary:
LOGAN, Utah – Earlier this week, Washington State coach Kirby Moore made the right move.

In announcing that he is taking over the Cougars’ playcalling duties, taking them away from a longtime friend in offensive coordinator Matt Miller, Moore demonstrated his understanding of the urgency of the moment. The Cougars’ offense has been floundering. Something had to change.

But will that be enough to help WSU secure a road win over Utah State on Friday night, set for 6 p.m. on the CW? All kinds of things could unfold, but here’s predicting the answer will be no, leading to an Aggie victory.

It will be fascinating to see what kinds of effects Moore’s control over this offense will have. Quarterback Caden Pinnick could look much sharper and much cleaner, avoiding the turnover problems that have plagued him early in his WSU career. But if the issues have less to do with playcalling and more to do with Pinnick himself, it’s possible he looks the same, which would make it exceedingly difficult for the Cougars (1-4, 0-1 Pac-12) to earn a win.

To be clear, WSU’s offensive woes have hardly been all Pinnick’s fault. Receivers have dropped passes and run routes short of the sticks. Offensive linemen have not been perfect. And the Cougs have gotten very little in the passing game from their tight ends. Nobody in this unit should be absolved of blame.

But the head of the snake is the quarterback, and even if the Cougars make a change at that position, it’s hard to foresee this offense taking down a Utah State defense that ranks fifth in the Pac-12 in scoring defense. QB Owen Eshelman has yet to see the field in any meaningful capacity, and the athletic Julian Dugger would have to prove to the Aggies’ defense that he can hurt them with his arm.

It’s a tough spot for WSU, no matter which QB gets the majority of reps in Friday’s game.

Final score: Utah State 13, WSU 7

Washington State.title: Washington State's keys to victory against Utah State | 2-minute drill
Washington State.summary:
Washington State at Utah State

Friday, 6 p.m.

Line: Utah State favored by 5½

TV: KSKN Radio: 920-AM

Key matchup

WSU QB against the Utah State defense: Usually, we would analyze the WSU QB’s matchup against the Utah State defense, but it’s unclear who that will be. The Cougars might stick with Caden Pinnick, who has languished to the tune of six turnovers in his first five games, or they might switch it up. They might go with redshirt freshman Owen Eshelman, who has yet to play any meaningful snaps in his college career, or they might pivot to redshirt sophomore Julian Dugger, who has broken some nice runs but hasn’t proven much with his arm in his limited playing time as a college QB.

For the sake of analyzing something, let’s assume WSU is sticking with Pinnick. The biggest focus for Pinnick will have to be avoiding turnovers, which he has not done in a consistent way yet. He has thrown an interception in all five games so far, and he also lost a fumble against Arizona, accounting for the majority of the Cougars’ nine total turnovers.

But will coaches stick with Pinnick for the entire game? It’s possible that even if Pinnick starts, coaches keep him on a short leash, wary of the turnover and pocket-presence issues he has faced. If those come bubbling up again, look for Moore to pull the plug.

How the Cougs win…

Because of the instability WSU is facing on offense, look for its defense to swing this one. Utah State quarterbacks Grady Brosterhous and McCae Hillstead have taken 17 sacks combined, and they have combined for 10 interceptions, the most of any team in the country. That doesn’t just open up things for Cougar defensive ends Matyus McLain and Linus Zunk. It could also mean a big day for WSU’s secondary, namely Jaylen Thomas, who has two interceptions on the year.

How the Aggies win…

Utah State can win this game by preying on WSU’s offense, which looks anything but potent at the moment. Pass rushers Adonis Jackson and Jordan Pendleton have combined for two sacks on 16 pressures, meaning the WSU offensive line will have to keep its quarterback – whoever it is – clean and upright.

If the Aggies can generate a turnover or two, as the Cougar offense has been wont to offer up, they can likely get it done at home.

Key stat: Minus-5

Can a key stat be a negative number? That’s WSU’s turnover margin on the year, a key reason behind its slow 1-4 start to the season. Can the Cougars improve that number? Can their defense take advantage of Utah State’s turnover problems, which have resulted in a margin of minus-7? Those patterns may swing Friday’s game.

Quotable

“I think Coach (Moore) is a great play-caller,” WSU tight end Jack Pedersen said. “Obviously, he did a great job at Missouri. That’s why he’s here. That’s why he’s the head coach here at Washington State. I think he’s going to do an amazing job, and I think we’re all excited to just get back out there and get a new opportunity.”

Washington State.title: WSU should get boost with play-calling shift to Kirby Moore | Week 6 picks
Washington State.summary:
Welcome to the Hotline’s weekly picks against the point spread, published Thursdays throughout the regular season with a focus on the most intriguing matchups across the West and the top games nationally. Betting lines are courtesy of VegasInsider.com unless noted otherwise. (Games involving FCS teams not included.) I went 7-5 last week and am 32-28-2 for the season. Picks are for entertainment purposes only … unless they aren’t.

Arizona coach Brent Brennan was having none of it. The long trip to Morgantown? The unusual practice routine with a Thursday flight? The early kickoff Saturday morning? No, no, no.

“If you let that be an excuse,” he told reporters, “it will be … And we are not in the excuse-making business.”

But the Hotline is in the excuse-making business, if you view disrupted circadian rhythms and altered brain chemistry as excuses.

We don’t. We view 1,800-mile flights across three time zones and 9 a.m. body-clock kickoffs as legitimate competitive obstacles in the post-realignment world of college football.

It’s not easy for East Coast teams to fly west and play late, at 7:30 p.m. Pacific. But it’s far more challenging for teams in the Pacific time zone to travel east, lose three hours and play at noon.

The data agrees.

For context on the RichRod Bowl, with Arizona facing its former coach, Rich Rodriguez, the Hotline examined how the former Pac-12 teams have fared in 9 a.m. kickoffs.

Of course, there is some nuance to the situation.

Should we consider Utah’s results in early games played in the Eastern time zone? That’s 10 a.m. for the Utes.

And what about Pacific time zone teams playing early games in Texas, which is only halfway across the country?

You could slice and dice the logistics a half-dozen ways.

We chose to keep things simple: How have the former Pac-12 schools fared in conference road games that start at 9 a.m. Pacific – exactly the circumstance Arizona is facing this weekend.

And in case there is any confusion, we did not evaluate the results based on wins and losses. The Hotline is no place for moral rectitude. We examined the results from a wagering perspective: How frequently did the traveling teams cover the point spread?

(Arizona is favored by three points, by the way.)

The research found that Arizona, Arizona State, USC, UCLA, Cal, Stanford, Oregon, Washington, Utah, Colorado and BYU – yes, we included BYU – have covered the spread seven times, failed to cover the spread 14 times and pushed (tied) once.

Yep: The teams are 7-14-1 against the spread when playing at 9 a.m., or 33.3%.

Which is telling, because the spread is designed to create 50-50 outcomes.

Given that the sample size (22 games) isn’t tiny and spans two-and-a-half seasons, that success rate of 33.3% suggests playing at 9 a.m. is, well, difficult.

That doesn’t mean the Wildcats are doomed – that they won’t cover the spread or, ahem, win the game.

In fact, Arizona managed the logistics very well the last time it faced this situation: the 30-24 victory at Cincinnati last November. Of course, the kickoff was technically at 10 a.m. because daylight saving time had ended two weeks earlier and Arizona, which skips the annual clock change, was only two hours behind Eastern time.

Did that hour matter? Not as much as Noah Fifita’s efficient play from the pocket or Arizona’s 50% conversion rate on third down or Cincinnati’s two turnovers.

And if those dynamics are in play Saturday morning, the Wildcats should leave Morgantown with their fifth victory of the season despite their depleted receiver corps.

But that performance (covering the spread and winning the game) was unusual for the former Pac-12 teams. Body clock disruption is real, and we would not be surprised if the Wildcats are not themselves Saturday morning, at least in the first half.

The trend is your friend, and the trend is screaming from the rooftop: Take the points.

To the picks …

Iowa (+31/2

) at Washington

Kickoff: Friday at 6 p.m. on Fox

Comment: The Hawkeyes are making a long trip on a short week after playing Michigan and Ohio State back-to-back, and quarterback Hank Brown’s status is uncertain because of a bad shoulder. Advantage Huskies? Yes, for sure. This stands as the defining game of their season. We absolutely love the under (411/2). Pick: Washington

Washington State (+51/2

) at Utah State

Kickoff: Friday at 6 p.m. on the CW

Comment: WSU first-year coach Kirby Moore has taken over play-calling duties, and we expect that to provide an immediate boost to what had been an inept unit. There are plenty of longer-term questions about the Cougars and their new coaching staff. But the defense is solid, and Utah State is flawed everywhere. Pick: Washington State

Iowa State (+10) at BYU

Kickoff: Friday at 7:15 p.m. on ESPN

Comment: The Cougars are without injured tailback LJ Martin but have their quarterback, Bear Bachmeier, plus a stout defense and enough moxie for two teams. Meanwhile, the Cyclones have a short week to recover from the emotional high of their win over West Virginia (45-42). One team is not like the other. Pick: BYU

Indiana (-71/2

) at Nebraska

Kickoff: 9 a.m on Fox

Comment: The Cornhuskers are undefeated but have played a soft schedule and, in no way, shape or form, are they ready for the Curt Cignetti smoke. Close early, not close late. Pick: Indiana

Arizona (-3) at West Virginia

Kickoff: 9 a.m. on TNT

Comment: The Wildcats shut down Cincinnati’s ground game last week, but the Mountaineers have a better scheme and a more dynamic quarterback in Michael Hawkins. Add the long flight, early kickoff and the absence of receiver Tre Spivey (broken foot) and this constitutes, by far, the greatest challenge for Arizona since the Week 2 trip to Provo. Pick: West Virginia

UCF (+91/2

) at Oklahoma State

Kickoff: 9 a.m. on ESPN2

Comment: The Knights lost at Houston last weekend and are back on the road to face a talented host that had two weeks to prepare. The Cowboys’ competitive advantage is immense. Pick: Oklahoma State

Texas (-8) vs. Oklahoma (In Dallas)

Kickoff: 12:30 on ABC

Comment: The only reasons to side with the Sooners are the X factor present in every Red River showdown and their stout defense. All other components suggest a lopsided victory for the Longhorns. Pick: Texas

UCLA (+111/2

) at Oregon

Kickoff: 12:30 p.m. on CBS

Comment: The Bruins have received a tad too much praise for their undefeated record considering all four victims have losing records. Yes, they are much improved under first-year coach Bob Chesney. But are they ready for Oregon’s personnel and the Autzen Stadium bedlam? Not in our view, especially with an offense that is overly reliant on the running game. We like the Ducks, who are expected to start Dylan Raiola at quarterback. Pick: Oregon

Virginia Tech (-10) at Cal

Kickoff: 12:30 p.m. on ACC Network

Comment: The Bears changed offensive play-callers in the middle of their loss to UNLV last weekend and have major issues with their defense and discipline. (They are one of the most penalized teams in the country.) Also, quarterback Jaron-Keawe Sagapolutele is in concussion protocol. But this is far too many points for a road team traveling across the country, especially given the rosters have comparable talent. Pick: Cal

San Diego State (+141/2

) at Oregon State

Kickoff: 3 p.m. on USA Network

Comment: Call this a funny-feeling pick. We don’t expect the Aztecs to win – they simply don’t have enough offense or a healthy enough roster – but it feels like the Beavers are due to experience some misfortune and unexpected resistance. Pick: San Diego State

USC (+11/2

) at Penn State

Kickoff: 4:30 p.m. on NBC

Comment: Two desperate blue bloods in a White Out game in Beaver Stadium? Yes, please. The Trojans are in must-win mode to remain on track for the playoff, while the Nittany Lions have lost two in a row (to Wisconsin and Northwestern). The hosts have a roster filled with transfers from Iowa State. The visitors have a roster filled with blue chippers. Pick: USC

Georgia (+2) at Alabama

Kickoff: 4:30 p.m. on ABC

Comment: One of the most anticipated games of the year with Alabama’s sensational quarterback, Keelon Russell, facing the mighty Bulldogs defense. If the College Football Playoff expands to 24 teams, showdowns like this would lose much of their do-or-die drama. Pick: Georgia

Hawaii (+201/2

) at Arizona State

Kickoff: 6:30 p.m. on FS1

Comment: Arizona State coach Kenny Dillingham has turned over play-calling responsibility to offensive coordinator Marcus Arroyo in the wake of a blowout home loss to Baylor. That could help, but the Sun Devils will benefit greatly from being back in their routine after the massive disruption caused by the London trip. Pick: Arizona State

Kansas (+15) at Utah

Kickoff: 7:15 p.m. on ESPN

Comment: The Utes are particularly difficult to handle in night games at Rice-Eccles. To that advantage, add two weeks to prepare, their ultra-dynamic offense and a highly flawed opponent. This shouldn’t be close when the fourth quarter begins. Heck, it might not be close when the second quarter ends. Pick: Utah

Boise State (-61/2

) at Fresno State

Kickoff: 7:30 p.m. on the CW

Comment: A huge game in the rebuilt Pac-12 between two title contenders and at least one CFP hopeful (Boise State). The Bulldogs’ defense is solid, but their offense is merely mediocre. And mediocre doesn’t work against the well-balanced Broncos, who should take control in the fourth quarter. Pick: Boise State

Straight-up winners: Washington, Washington State, BYU, Indiana, West Virginia, Oklahoma State, Oregon, Virginia Tech, Texas, Oregon State, USC, Georgia, Arizona State, Utah and Boise State

Five-star special: Oklahoma State. There is perhaps no tougher assignment in the sport than playing back-to-back road games, with the second game against a team coming off a bye. That is UCF’s fate against the Cowboys.

Washington State.title: WA prep football players to sport special helmet stickers this week. Here's why
Washington State.summary:
High school football teams across Washington will be donning a special helmet sticker in this week’s games to raise mental health awareness.

The Washington State Football Coaches Association (WSFCA) has partnered with Hilinski’s Hope, a foundation founded in 2018 by Mark and Kym Hilinski to honor the life of their son Tyler Hilinski – a Washington State quarterback who wore jersey No. 3 and died by suicide, despite showing no visible signs of struggle.

“We’ve mailed out 20,000-ish helmet stickers across the state so that coaches can distribute them to their players and start the conversation about why they’re putting the stickers on their helmets,” said Tumwater football coach Willie Garrow, who also serves as a secretary for the WSFCA.

The WSFCA also partnered with the Seattle Seahawks. Offensive lineman Abe Lucas, who played at WSU, recorded a video that high school football coaches will be showing to their teams. There will also be a 10-second moment of silence at the beginning of the third quarter of varsity games across the state.

The aim of the actions is to continue to raise awareness, break down the stigma around mental illness, and put real resources in the hands of student-athletes nationwide, according to the WSFCA.

Garrow said the partnership with the Hilinski’s Hope foundation has turned into good conversations with his team, and hopefully, with teams across the state.

“This was a good incentive to start that process, start the conversation,” Garrow said. “For as much as high school football gets blown up into scores, games, who wins and loses, ultimately we’re still dealing with 50 to 100 14-to-18-year-old boys. It’s a good reminder that we have a greater responsibility than blocking and tackling.

“As an association and as coaches, trying to remind guys and reinforce those good conversations, make sure guys are making it a priority.”

Washington State.title: What role has WSU's offensive line played in the Cougars' struggling offense?
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – Ashton Tripp is a man of few words, a giant Washington State offensive lineman whose height belies his desire to chat. He’s been around the Cougars’ program for more than three years now, and in his second year starting at left tackle, he’s never been long on words.

So it follows that Tripp, a 6-foot-7 product of Kennewick, has been succinct in summarizing his WSU offense’s struggles so far.

“After watching the tape, I mean, it’s disappointing for sure,” Tripp said on Monday. “We gotta play 11 as one. I know it’s cliche, but that’s just how it’s gotta be. Here and there, it’s always one guy off, so we just gotta click.”

Much has been made of WSU’s offensive woes, the struggles from quarterback Caden Pinnick that have played an outsize role in his team’s 1-4 start to the season, especially his offense’s output of 11.8 points per game – No. 130 nationally. Headed into a Friday night matchup with Utah State, an evening kickoff in Logan, coach Kirby Moore is taking over playcalling duties to try and revive a moribund outfit.

Pinnick has shouldered much of the blame, and plenty has been deserved. He’s thrown an interception in all five games, and he’s lost six total turnovers, accounting for the majority of the Cougs’ nine total turnovers. On Monday, Moore seemed to indicate that he is open to making a change at that position, perhaps moving toward redshirt sophomore Julian Dugger or redshirt freshman Owen Eshelman.

“Everyone’s gonna get reps,” Moore said. “I think that’s the most important thing. Everyone’s gotta make the reps count. We’ll see where it’s at on Friday, and we’ll play ball.”

On the topic of WSU’s scuffling offense, here is a subplot that has gone a little understated: How has the Cougars’ offensive line played? Tripp has acquitted himself well, but things haven’t gone as smoothly on other parts of their front five, leading coaches to make a few personnel changes after WSU’s road loss to Kansas State last month.

In the three games since, coaches have rolled with this group: Tripp at left tackle, Jonny Lester at left guard, Noah Dunham at center, Nick Bakken at right guard and Jaylin Caldwell at right tackle. At the beginning of the season, Lester was playing right tackle, but after the K-State game, left guard Kyle Martin was benched, prompting Lester to move to left guard – where he started last season – and pulling Caldwell off the bench to play right tackle.

Could WSU make changes to that group? Moore has said that everything with the Cougars’ offense is up for reevaluation, which could open up the door for veteran tackle Maximus McCree, whose transfer was hailed as a key acquisition for WSU back in January. A former starter at Washington, he has yet to play a snap at WSU.

As currently constructed, how has WSU’s offensive line fared? In WSU’s 26-6 loss to Fresno State last weekend, Pinnick took five sacks, giving him 18 on the season, which ranks No. 129 of 138 FBS teams nationally. But interestingly, Pro Football Focus only dinged the Cougars’ offensive line for three of those, indicating that Pinnick was responsible for the other two. That would add up to the eye test, which has affirmed that Pinnick’s pocket presence ranks highly on his list of problems.

In fact, here’s a key trend to consider: PFF has a stat called QB-fault pressures, which are basically what they sound like. In simplest terms, these are sacks that PFF determines were the QB’s fault rather than the offensive line’s – he ran himself into pressure, held onto the ball too long, something of that sort.

Pinnick ranks first nationally with 10 QB-fault sacks.

That goes a long way in explaining some patterns, like his inability to make timely decisions and find the right balance of staying in the pocket too long and bailing too quickly. But to a certain degree, it absolves the Cougars’ offensive line of blame, revealing Pinnick to be more of a culprit for his own sacks than the men charged with protecting him.

But the Cougars’ front five haven’t been perfect, either. Dunham has been the least responsible for QB pressures, according to PFF, only 9% of the pressures Pinnick has faced coming from his assignments. That lines up with his season as a whole, earning the offensive line’s top pass-blocking grade (65.9) and only six pressures total.

Most of the pressure Pinnick has faced has come from the right side, with Bakken and Caldwell sharing about 22% each of pressures. Lester has the same rate, while the lowest belongs to Tripp, at just 17%.

What about run-blocking? Another reason the Cougars are struggling on offense is their lack of a credible running game. In the second half against Fresno State, tailbacks Maxwell Woods, Kirby Vorhees and Leo Pulalasi combined for just five carries. This week, Moore emphasized the need to incorporate them more into the Cougs’ offense.

The highest-graded run-blocker on the WSU offensive line is Lester, who has earned a grade of 74.6, well above average. Next is Caldwell at 61.1, while Bakken is at 60.1, Dunham is at 55.3 and Tripp checks in at the lowest grade with 51.6. It’s important to note that Lester, Dunham and Tripp were all recruited to play in a much different offense, much closer to the Air Raid of old than the approach these current Cougs are taking.

“It’s just all about us. I just keep coming back to it,” Tripp said. “We gotta just keep doing more. We gotta keep working, keep doing extra stuff, get the guys together, and we gotta start clicking.”

Washington State.title: Sizzling Oregon State, struggling WSU and eligibility complications | Pac-12 bowl projections
Washington State.summary:
The Pac-12 bowl selection process in 2026 treats the former conference as if it never imploded, grouping the 12 legacy schools together just as it did the previous two years. Meanwhile, the new Pac-12 teams have separate postseason arrangements. To simplify the situation, we have split the 18 teams into two groups: Pac-12 legacy bowls and Pac-12 new bowls. Washington State and Oregon State are part of the legacy bowl process with the exception of the Poinsettia Bowl. 

So low was the bar for Oregon State this fall that its 3-2 record constitutes an upside surprise of the highest order.

Whether it’s the closer-than-expected losses or the resounding wins, the dazzling aerial game or coach JaMarcus Shephard’s unstoppable enthusiasm, the Beavers have produced a riveting narrative entering the midway point of the season.

They have also turned trigonometry into basic multiplication.

Oregon State’s bowl math is easy enough to compute: If they win three of the seven remaining games, the Beavers will participate in the postseason for the first time since 2023 and the fourth time in the past decade.

But which bowl?

That’s where the situation turns complicated because the Beavers, like fellow Pac-12 holdover Washington State, are eligible for two sets of games: The legacy Pac-12 bowls and the new Pac-12 bowls.

And for the College Football Playoff, of course.

That sentence might have read like fantasy in August but is worth brief mention here. If the Beavers somehow run the table, win the Pac-12 and finish 11-2, with competitive losses to Texas Tech and Houston and at least one victory over Boise State, they would receive consideration for the Group of Six berth in the CFP.

That scenario has a non-zero chance of materializing, but not by much.

According to projections on teamrankings.com, the wagering and analytics website, the likelihood of Oregon State winning out is about 2 percent.

But what if the Beavers finish 7-5 or 8-4? Where might they land? More significantly, would they be placed in the pool of legacy Pac-12 games or new Pac-12 games?

The key elements to the process are as follows:

• The legacy Pac-12 teams are eligible for (in order) the Alamo, Las Vegas, Holiday, Sun, Poinsettia and Independence Bowls.

• The six new Pac-12 teams are eligible for the Poinsettia and Hawaii Bowls, plus a pool of ESPN games.

• Oregon State and Washington State will participate on the legacy Pac-12 side of all games except the Poinsettia pairing, where they are considered new Pac-12 teams.

• The Pac-12 legacy bowls select first, meaning the Beavers likely would land in a legacy game if they are 8-4 or 9-3. If they only win six or seven games, there’s a chance they would not be picked for the legacy games and move over to the Poinsettia or Hawaii Bowls.

• Don’t forget about the one-win-down rule, which allows any of the legacy bowls to pass one team in favor of another as long as there is no more than a one-game difference in record. The Holiday Bowl, for example, could pass on the Beavers at 8-4 in favor of Washington at 7-5 but not if the Huskies are 6-6.

That policy could work against the Beavers because of their small media market and low national profile.

It could work in favor of the Beavers if bowl executives prioritize ticket sales and Oregon State fans are considered likely to attend the game en masse.

Even if we knew Oregon State’s final record, projecting a landing spot would be exceedingly difficult because of the myriad factors involved.

Also, we don’t know how many, if any, legacy Pac-12 teams will jump into the CFP, thereby opening spots in the non-playoff games. If Utah and/or Oregon qualify, everyone below them in the pecking order moves up.

However, it’s reasonable to assume only a handful of legacy Pac-12 teams will finish with eight or more wins based on current records and upcoming schedules.

If the Beavers are 9-3 or 8-4, they would be well positioned for the Holiday or Sun Bowls.

Why not the Alamo or Las Vegas? Both could be options, but the one-win-down rule might prompt the bowls to select one of the Los Angeles schools.

If the Beavers are 7-5, the Sun or Independence Bowls would come into play.

Only at 6-6 would a berth in Poinsettia, as a new Pac-12 team, become the most realistic option.

In some ways, that might be the most interesting matchup. We would love to see Braden Atkinson and Jesse Legree face Washington or Arizona.

To the bowl projections …

Pac-12 legacy bowls

College Football Playoff: Utah (Big 12 champion)

Comment: The Utes (4-0) could qualify for the CFP through the at-large pool if they finish with one loss. (It’s tough to envision a two-loss Big 12 team getting the requisite respect from the selection committee.) For the moment, we view Utah as the team to beat in the conference, particularly with Texas Tech looking vulnerable on a weekly basis.

College Football Playoff: Oregon (Big Ten at-large)

Comment: The Ducks (3-1) have eight games remaining, one loss in their pocket and a date in Columbus looming. At 10-2, an at-large bid should be forthcoming, although they might not be seeded high enough to host an opening-round game.

Alamo Bowl: UCLA

Comment: There is a good chance the UCLA-USC duel at the end of the season determines bowl destinations for both teams, with the winner receiving the more prestigious assignment. Given the upcoming schedules, the Bruins (4-0) have a better chance to sneak into the CFP, but the best non-playoff bowl is the most likely option at this point.

Las Vegas Bowl: USC

Comment: The schedule includes Wisconsin, Indiana and UCLA on the road and Ohio State at home. Those teams are a combined 17-2. Even if the Trojans (5-1) split that brutal quartet, they would finish with three losses. And the committee has never invited a 9-3 team to the playoff party.

Holiday Bowl: Oregon State

Comment: The Beavers (3-2) would celebrate a bowl bid anywhere. Yuma, Elko, Yakima – sign them up! But San Diego against an ACC opponent? Corvallis would become a ghost town the last week of December.

Sun Bowl: Arizona

Comment: Don’t dismiss the Wildcats (4-1) as a title contender in the Big 12 race, particularly after they whacked Cincinnati. But if they don’t reach Arlington, options could be limited: The L.A. schools might have priority for the Alamo and Las Vegas Bowls (TV markets), and Arizona was in the Holiday last year.

Poinsettia Bowl: Washington

Comment: A victory over Iowa on Friday night is important but not critical for the bowl math given the spate of winnable games remaining. But the reeling Huskies (3-2) won’t be a popular pick on the bowl circuit. Executives always favor teams with energized, not depressed, fans.

Independence Bowl: Arizona State

Comment: The Hotline supercomputer ran 10,000 simulations and spit out a 6-6 record for the Sun Devils 5,001 times. Just kidding. We don’t have a supercomputer. But we do have eyes. And from what we saw of Arizona State (2-2) over the weekend, six wins looks right.

Non-qualifier: Cal

Comment: Had you mapped the worst possible scenario for a new coach in Berkeley, it would effectively match Tosh Lupoi’s opening month. The Bears (2-3) will be lucky to win five games, much less six or seven.

Non-qualifier: Colorado

Comment: The Buffaloes (2-3) are averaging 10.3 points per game against FBS opponents. Barring a court order that gives Shedeur Sanders additional eligibility, the trajectory won’t change enough for CU to win four of the remaining seven.

Non-qualifier: Stanford

Comment: We aren’t aware of an NCAA policy banning any team that loses to Wake Forest by 54 points from participating in the postseason. But it would make more sense than most of the organization’s rules. In our view , Stanford (2-3) is essentially playing for 2028.

Non-qualifier: Washington State

Comment: First-year coach Kirby Moore is taking over play-calling duties for the struggling Cougars (1-4), which essentially means he picked the wrong offensive coordinator and the wrong quarterback. At least Moore got the defense right with coordinator Trent Bray.

Pac-12 new bowls

College Football Playoff: Boise State

Comment: At this point, the Broncos (4-1) hold the pole position in the race for the Group of Six spot in the playoff, with New Mexico, James Madison and Toledo as the top competition. Yes, North Dakota State is undefeated, but we aren’t convinced the Bison warrant that level of respect. Their schedule has been pillowy soft.

Poinsettia Bowl: Fresno State

Comment: A morsel of clarity will come to the Pac-12 race Saturday night when the Bulldogs (4-1) host Boise State in the first of three games matching the presumptive title contenders. And for what it’s worth, Fresno State also gets Oregon State at home.

Hawaii Bowl: San Diego State

Comment: The Aztecs (2-3) showed enough grit to beat Texas State, despite a roster torched by injury and illness (i.e., the mumps outbreak), that we have upgraded their forecast. But to make the bowl math work, they might need help from the conference’s Flex schedule. Five wins entering the final weekend is a distinct possibility.

Non-qualifier: Colorado State

Comment: If Jim Mora had changed defensive playcallers prior to the UTSA game, the Rams (2-3) might be on the high side of .500 right now and in prime position for a bowl berth. They have more than enough offense to secure six wins.

Non-qualifier: Texas State

Comment: The loss in San Diego, to a depleted opponent, could cost the Bobcats (2-3) a bowl bid. Of course, we could say the same about their come-from-ahead defeat to UTSA, as well.

Non-qualifier: Utah State

Comment: The Hotline saw a comment from Nevada coach Jeff Choate about the Mountain West being superior to the Pac-12. At the top, New Mexico could very well be a match for Boise State. But the middle and bottom tiers of the Pac-12, including Utah State (1-4), are far superior. Just check the scoreboard.

Washington State.title: Gap between WSU, conference leaders looks massive | Pac-12 power rankings Week 6
Washington State.summary:
Editor’s note: The Pac-12 football power rankings are published each Sunday and consider both the latest results and seasonlong performance. Call it an objectively subjective look at the state of the conference. If you’re unhappy with the order, email us at the address below … or play better. For comparative purposes, we have included the placement of each team in last week’s rankings.

One week into round-robin play, it’s abundantly clear: The Pac-12 is a three-team race.

Boise State, Oregon State and Fresno State are the class of the conference, and it doesn’t appear to be particularly close. The gap between the top three and bottom five feels like a chasm.

Washington State doesn’t have enough offense to secure a bowl berth, much less contend for a spot in the Pac-12 championship game.

Colorado State doesn’t have enough defense. (Nor do the Rams have a defensive coordinator at the moment).

San Diego State? The Aztecs are lacking the most essential ingredient: healthy bodies.

Texas State doesn’t do anything well enough, which is doubly true when it comes to holding second-half leads.

Utah State does everything poorly.

That’s it. Remove those five flawed teams, and you have three remaining.

They aren’t created equal, not by any stretch: The Beavers lead with their offense, the Bulldogs with their defense and the Broncos with both, which explains their status as the frontrunner for both the Pac-12 title and a berth in the College Football Playoff.

But the beauty of the rebuilt Pac-12’s small size is the pure round-robin schedule. We don’t have to imagine how one contender would fare against another or delay judgment until the conference championship game.

In the Big 12, Utah and BYU don’t play Texas Tech.

In the SEC, Alabama and Georgia don’t play Texas.

In the Big Ten, Oregon doesn’t play Indiana.

But the Pac-12 doesn’t have that problem with eight teams and seven league games.

Everyone plays everyone, allowing us to identify the defining dates:

Oct. 10: Boise State at Fresno State

Oct. 31: Oregon State at Fresno State

Nov. 14: Oregon State at Boise State

Advantage to the Bulldogs, right? They host the other two while Oregon State is on the road for both.

Not necessarily.

Oregon State has played well away from home, with blowout victories at UTEP and Colorado State and a competitive loss at Houston.

Boise State can win anywhere.

Here are the victory projections for each team against the other two, according to the gambling and analytics website TeamRankings.com:

• Boise State: 66.3% at Fresno State and 77.4% against Oregon State

• Fresno State: 36.7% against Boise State and 59% against Oregon State

• Oregon State: 22.6% at Boise State and 41% at Fresno State

Our hunch: The Broncos win both, the Beavers split and the Bulldogs get swept.

As the late, great philosopher Bill Walton said often, “Offense wins championships.”

To the power rankings …

(All times Pacific)

1. Boise State (4-1/1-0)

Result: beat Utah State 37-18

Next up: at Fresno State (7:30 p.m. on the CW)

Comment: No team in the conference has better balance than the Broncos – not only offense-defense balance but also run-pass balance: They are averaging 227 rushing yards and 212 passing yards per game and likely will need every bit of both Saturday night against the Bulldogs, who allow just 16 points per game. (Last week: 1)

2. Oregon State (3-2/1-0)

Result: won at Colorado State 56-26

Next up: vs. San Diego State (3 p.m. on USA Network)

Comment: Receiver Jesse Legree falls into the same where-did-they-find-that-guy category as former Oregon State stars like Brandin Cooks and Jacquizz Rodgers. (The answer is Baltimore). But as the heart of conference play ramps up and opponents develop a better sense for OSU’s scheme and formations, we wonder: How will the Beavers adjust to the adjustments? (Last week: 2)

3. Fresno State (4-1/1-0)

Result: won at Washington State 26-6

Next up: vs. Boise State (7:30 p.m. on The CW)

Comment: The Bulldogs were set up to fail in the season opener at USC, which had already played (San Jose State) and was far sharper. Since that 39-0 loss, Fresno State is allowing 10.8 points per game. (Last week: 3)

4. Colorado State (2-3/0-1)

Result: lost to Oregon State 56-26

Next up: idle

Comment: It’s not often that a coordinator is stripped of his playcalling duties during a game. But if you had asked us to name the three Pac-12 head coaches most likely to make that type of in-game decision, Jim Mora Jr. would have been among our group. (Granted, relieving Tyson Summers of his responsibilities was a competitive imperative). (Last week: 4)

5. San Diego State (2-3/1-0)

Result: beat Texas State 31-29

Next up: at Oregon State (3 p.m. on USA Network)

Comment: An indisputably impressive victory for the Aztecs considering their two tailbacks were injured, more than a dozen players were unavailable due to the mumps outbreak and quarterback Jayden Denegal has struggled under any and every condition this season. And yet, the Aztecs rallied from a 14-point deficit thanks to their defense and special teams. (Last week: 7)

6. Texas State (2-3/0-1)

Result: lost at San Diego State 31-29

Next up: idle

Comment: The Bobcats were outscored 52-21 after halftime in losses to UTSA and San Diego State, dropping the former by five points and the latter by two. Had they held on, the season would have an entirely different look and feel. But one of the defining features of mediocre teams is the inability to close out games. (Last week: 5)

7. Washington State (1-4/0-1)

Result: lost to Fresno State 26-6

Next up: at Utah State (Friday at 6 p.m. on The CW)

Comment: From here, it’s clear that first-year coach Kirby Moore, a former receiver and offensive coordinator, has no answers. He announced Monday that he will take over the offensive playcalling duties. It’s clear that if Moore doesn’t fix the offensive offense in the next 19 games, Washington State will be in the market for a new coach. Time is short when attempting to prove you belong in the Power Four. (Last week: 6)

8. Utah State (1-4/0-1)

Result: lost at Boise State 37-18

Next up: vs. Washington State (Friday at 6 p.m. on The CW)

Comment: One team will collect its second victory of the season Friday night in Logan, but the process could be tough on the eyes and set the sport back years. First team to 11 wins. (Last week: 8)
